analysis.one_liner: Blocks Medicare from using AI-assisted prior authorization to deny or delay care in traditional Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced December 2, 2025 with 3 cosponsors, sits in two House committees with no action scheduled since.
analysis.plain_summary: Traditional Medicare has never required doctors to get approval before providing care. In 2025, Medicare announced a test program (WISeR) that would bring prior authorization—including AI-assisted review—into traditional Medicare for some services. This bill would stop that program and permanently bar Medicare from testing any prior authorization model, including AI-based ones, for services covered under traditional Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and people with disabilities on traditional Medicare, who would not face new pre-approval requirements that can delay or deny medically necessary care, plus the doctors and hospitals that would otherwise absorb the added paperwork and the risk of unpaid claims.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the implementation of the WISeR prior authorization model announced in July 2025, and any substantially similar model.

Amends the law governing Medicare payment demonstrations so the Secretary may never select a model that adds prior authorization, including through artificial intelligence, for services covered under traditional Medicare.

analysis.who_pays: Prior authorization vendors and insurers who stood to profit from administering the WISeR model, plus CMS's ability to test new cost-saving tools; any reduction in inappropriate services the model might have achieved would not be realized.

drawbacks.text: The WISeR model was justified as a way to reduce wasteful and inappropriate services in traditional Medicare; blocking it means forfeiting whatever savings and reduced overuse it might have produced.
The bill permanently forecloses Medicare from testing any prior authorization approach in traditional Medicare, even less aggressive designs, limiting the agency's flexibility to try cost controls.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients and doctors, the benefit is concrete: no new pre-approval gates between them and Medicare-covered care, a change many clinicians argue prevents delays and denials of needed care. The cost is that Medicare loses a test of a tool meant to trim inappropriate services, so any waste remains unchecked. The bill protects patients against a known harm while giving up an uncertain savings experiment; the tradeoff favors beneficiaries, but the design is absolute rather than conditional.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, where nothing has happened yet.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on December 2, 2025 by Rep. Greg Landsman.
It was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
It has 3 cosponsors, all House Democrats.
No further action, hearing, or vote has been taken since referral, and the Congress is still in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the scheduled WISeR prior authorization experiment proceeds unimpeded; vendors and insurers positioned to administer it keep their planned role, while traditional Medicare patients face the new pre-approval requirements it would bring.

for.name: Rep. Greg Landsman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar AI-assisted prior authorization in traditional Medicare.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter named so far is a House Democrat, but no one has opposed it yet—the bill has not moved past committee referral, so no opposition is on the record.

industries.industry: Prior authorization vendors and health insurers
industries.note: The WISeR model would let vendors administer pre-approval for traditional Medicare services and share in savings from denied or reduced care. The bill eliminates that market opportunity; its profit mechanism—getting paid when care is withheld—runs against patients' access to care.

industries.industry: Doctors, hospitals, and clinicians in traditional Medicare
industries.note: They would avoid new pre-approval paperwork and the risk of claims denied after care is delivered. Their interest in the bill matches patients' interest in timely treatment.

analysis.trajectory: With 3 cosponsors, dual referral to two committees, and no hearing or markup on record, a standalone floor vote is unlikely this session. The realistic path is attaching the language to a larger Medicare or spending package, or reintroduction if it dies.
